fixes.explanation: An advance is pay handed over before the work, friend, and that would be a fun Friday. But Paul says the wages of the worker are “…not credited as a gift, but as an obligation.” He means what the worker is owed for work already done.

Yes, friend. Paul says, “Now the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation.” If you put in the hours, the pay is owed to you. That's why nobody throws a surprise party when payday shows up.

Hard work earns wages, friend, and Paul just covered that in verse 4. Here he pictures someone who “…does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly…” So what God justifies in this verse is the ungodly, and that person's faith is what gets credited as righteousness.

That's right, friend. Paul quotes David, king of Israel, who says, “Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered.” Forgiven and covered, in the same breath. I spent years covered in dust in the back of a junk drawer, but this kind of covered is much better.

That's the order you'd guess if circumcision was the thing doing the work, friend. But Paul answers his own question: “It was not after, but before.” He says Abraham received the sign of circumcision as a seal of “…the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised.” (Romans 4:11)
Fasting isn't anywhere in this verse, friend. Paul says Abraham is “…the father of all who believe but are not circumcised…” Believing is the word that fits the blank.

Canaan is a good guess for a place tied to Abraham, friend, since he did set out for that land (Genesis 12:5). But Paul doesn't mention land in this verse. He says the circumcised are also his children when they “…walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.” It's about his faith, not an address.

Earned fits the way the law-livers might see it, friend. But the verse says, “…faith is useless and the promise is worthless…” Paul uses “worthless” for what the promise would be if the heirs are those who live by the law.
Paul says it outright, friend: “…the law brings wrath.” He follows it with, “And where there is no law, there is no transgression.” So the statement is True, and it's a heavy line to read.
Yes, friend. Paul says the promise comes by faith “…so that it may rest on grace…” Grace is what the promise rests on. That's a solid place to stand.

That one shrinks the list, friend. Paul says the promise is guaranteed to all Abraham’s offspring, “…not only to those who are of the law, but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham.” The words are not only. It goes wider than the law.
Yes, friend. Paul calls Him “…the God who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist.” Think about that for a second. That's the God Abraham believed.

Humbled is a word that could fit, friend, but it isn't Paul's. He says Abraham “…did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God…” Strengthened is the word.
That's right, friend. Paul says Abraham was “…fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised.” His confidence was in what God was able to do. That's a very sturdy place to put it.

That's the one, friend. Paul says Jesus “…was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification.” He was delivered over for our trespasses, and He was raised for our justification. Paul puts both halves in one sentence, and I love that.
